claim: beam_disc's lit-arc cap of 10 berths means night 1 (6 intact facets, quota 8) already covers 10 of 12 berths from one fixed disc position, so the teaching night barely requires rotating the beam at all — the game's central mechanic goes essentially untested on the night it's supposed to be taught.
where: Turn structure > Sweep; Action economy > Maximum lit arc
fix_tried: Lower the lit-arc cap from 10 to 6 berths (half the ring). Facet counts 4-6 (nights 1-3), which currently give 8, 10, 10, all flatten to 6; facet counts 1-3 are already <=6 and untouched. Now the pointer's position matters from turn 1 instead of only once the disc has narrowed.

claim: rank_track never gates or changes a rule — it only totals a number the harbour headcount already shows at every dawn and reports it once at campaign end, which is precisely the 'earns no decision of its own' test the design already used to fold relay_socket into a molded feature instead of a part.
fix_tried: Give the slider a read that feeds back into play: e.g. if it sits behind the pace needed for 'the light held' by night 4's dawn, the crew may spend 1 extra charge on a flare that night. If no such hook is wanted, cut the part and report the same end-title off a tally kept on paper beside the plinth.

claim: The 5-word, no-numbers muzzle on non-active keepers only applies 'during this whole turn,' so nothing stops the table from openly dictating the exact rotate/dwell sequence in full sentences the instant the previous turn's Relay phase ends — a confident keeper can hand off a fully solved play, and the muzzle only blocks real-time backseat driving, not the decision itself.
fix_tried: Extend the silence to cover the handoff: from the moment dawn_ratchet advances in Relay until the new lamp holder clicks it home in Watch, every other keeper may say at most 5 words, no chained clauses, no numbers — closing the gap between turns where the plan currently gets dictated in full.

A player reduced to zero markers cannot use Move or Press and, once all seven sockets are occupied, may spend the rest of the session taking consolation points instead of playing the map, which is effective early elimination from the core game.
where: Turn structure — Claim, Move, and Press; player_markers
fix_tried: Add Emergency Entry: when a player controls no markers, they may activate any Claim, Move, or Press tile to place one reserve marker in an empty socket, or if the map is full, replace a rival marker on a value-1 outer socket at zero influence cost.

claim: The compulsory random legacy lock can remove six Claims or every copy of another action, collapsing later sessions into sparse or one-note play, while the ratchet_dial itself currently asks no player to make a decision.
fix_tried: Before each click, reveal candidates until two are eligible, where eligible means its removal leaves at least 6 Claim, 4 Move, 4 Press, and 2 Gain tiles unlocked; the lowest-influence player chooses one candidate to lock and all others return to the hopper.

claim: Gain's guaranteed 2 influence weakly dominates Move because a Move improves final socket value by at most 2 and usually only 1 while also opening the vacated socket, so the six Move tiles rarely create a real choice when Gain is held.
where: Turn structure — Move and Gain; ability_tiles
fix_tried: After resolving a legal Move, also gain 1 influence.

claim: Influence is both victory score and Press permission, so an early leader can afford repeated attacks while a trailer at 0 or 1 cannot attack at all, creating positive feedback that the lowest-player start rule does not reliably reverse.
fix_tried: Make Press cost 0 influence when its target has strictly more influence than the acting player and 2 influence when the target is tied or behind.

claim: The player acting last in round 5 can make an unanswered Press, and assigning first player to the lowest scorer gives that decisive final activation to the seat immediately before the intended catch-up player.
where: Setup — starting player; Turn structure — round 5
fix_tried: At the start of round 5, lock a special turn order from highest influence to lowest influence, breaking ties in reverse round-4 order, so the most-behind player receives the final response instead of a fixed neighboring seat.

claim: At four players the unchanged four-marker cap lets one lucky player occupy four of seven sockets, including every value-2-or-3 socket, leaving the other three players to share only the low-value remainder and amplifying early Claim luck.
where: Action economy — marker limit; player_markers; tile_set
fix_tried: Set the per-player socket cap by player count: 4 markers at 2 players, 3 at 3 players, and 2 at 4 players; treat Claim as unusable while at that cap.

claim: Because held tiles never refresh, a player can keep two scarce action types out of circulation for all five rounds, so the initial private deal becomes an unanswerable denial strategy as the legacy pool shrinks.
fix_tried: After each of rounds 1–4, have every player return both held tiles simultaneously, mix the hopper 10 times, and deal each player a fresh two-tile hand before the next round.

claim: The 0–120 influence track contains 54 unreachable spaces because even four optimal claims plus one Gain score at most 11 per session and 66 per campaign, so nearly half the component records no possible game state or decision.
fix_tried: Change each personal influence track and its full-track rule from 0–120 to 0–66.

claim: Once a service reaches four successes or three failures its result cannot change, and every positive bid can only add a fragment, so zero bids strictly dominate and up to three of the six turns become forced idle play.
fix_tried: End the service immediately when its fourth success or third failure is recorded, rather than always resolving six slugs.

claim: At four players the largest opening total that cannot overload the minimum demand is 6 and it covers only 5 of 12 slugs, while reaching the best possible 8-of-12 coverage requires total 10 and overloads 7 of 12 slugs, making the advertised four-player mode a damage trap even under perfect group allocation.
where: Setup — four-player task_slug demands; Resolve — overload limit
fix_tried: At four players only, calculate the overload limit as the lower of current capacity and printed demand plus 3; this makes total 7 safe against every intact-capacity slug and able to satisfy 7 of 12 demands.

claim: Because five and six won services both give Steady and any loss grants Recovery, a group with four early wins is safer deliberately bidding zero through service 5 and attempting its fifth win under Recovery in service 6 than trying to win both services normally.
where: Win/lose — service ending bands and Recovery orientation
fix_tried: Set service-ending bands to Steady at 6 wins, Scarred at 5, Rationed at 3–4, and Retired at 0–2, and grant Recovery only after a lost service that recorded exactly 3 successes.

claim: A fragment lowers capacity on the very next turn, which makes another overcommit more likely before Recovery can exist and can turn one mistake into an uncontrollable same-service march to fragment 6.
fix_tried: Snapshot current capacity at the start of each service and use that value for every turn in that service; newly installed fragments begin reducing capacity only when the next service starts.

claim: The fragment ratchet duplicates the exact 0–6 damage state already shown by the mandatory ordered wedges, so removing it would cost no decision and would also remove a possible desynchronization error.
fix_tried: Delete the fragment_ratchet, count installed wedges for damage, and print the alternating left/right tie arrow beside each of the six ordered wedge sockets.

claim: A normal early timeout can resolve two floods into every unclaimed compartment and install at least four caps at once, so one failed first dive can end the advertised 45-90 minute campaign at 0 successes.
fix_tried: On a lost dive install exactly 1 weld cap: after resolving all remaining slugs, the crew chooses 1 flooding open compartment to weld, then all other open flood dials reset to dry; the fourth failed dive therefore ends the campaign.

claim: Six successful dives do not end the campaign, so once the crew reaches 6 the dominant strategy is to stop playing and deliberately time out until the fourth cap releases the trophy.
fix_tried: End the campaign immediately when the success counter advances to 6, and change the trophy latch so it releases on either success 6 or the fourth installed weld cap.

claim: Because every compartment will receive exactly two floods, a 1-action Claim on its first flood always gives more protection than a 1-action Pump, making Pump merely the fallback used when no ready plug is available.
where: Action economy: Pump and Claim / wedge_plug / flood_slug
fix_tried: Make Claim legal only when the pawn's compartment is at 2 floods; it still costs 1 action and clears and protects the compartment, forcing a real choice between pumping the first flood now or risking the second flood to earn the plug's efficiency.

claim: The open board and deterministic two-slug threat let a confident player prescribe the next move during Handoff, so the current speech restriction pauses quarterbacking without preventing it.
fix_tried: Add: 'Only the active player may speak or gesture from Alarm through Handoff; their Handoff sentence may report what they did or observed but may not address a player or use an imperative.'

claim: The lowest-numbered pawn starts every dive and therefore repeatedly receives the extra turn whenever the 2-per-compartment alarm count is not divisible by the player count, creating persistent seat-based agency that no player action can answer.
fix_tried: Add a first-player marker; give it to a random player on dive 1 and pass it one seat clockwise after every dive, with its holder acting first regardless of pawn number.

claim: Weld caps five through eight are installed only after the fourth cap has already fixed the campaign result, so those four components add handling and cost without creating a decision.
fix_tried: Reduce weld_cap quantity from 8 to 4 and stop Collapse immediately after the fourth cap is installed.

claim: At three and four players every public tuple of starting districts uniquely identifies the chosen dispatch set, and the shared set letter on each private face makes that lookup still easier, so a repeat player can recover every supposedly private queue and refuge and quarterback the core puzzle; this is high because asymmetric information is the game's main protection against one-player control.
fix_tried: Remove set letters and rebuild the manifests so every public start tuple and every individual seat card occurs in at least four different matched sets with different partner routes; this costs route variety and requires revalidating all 48 sets and their balance tail.

claim: After the seventh delivery only one road remains open, so unless the next courier can make the eighth delivery, the seventh-book player must aim that sole road at the next seat and later seats are usually already doomed or forced to spend the last detours even though several turns may remain; this is high because the advertised 16-turn finish collapses into a brittle forced chain before the finale.
where: Turn structure phases 1, 4, and 5; peg; watch_wheel
fix_tried: Cap the Watch at six standing pegs: on the seventh and eighth deliveries relocate one standing peg into an empty hole instead of adding another, and remove the eighth-peg requirement from the win check; this costs the escalating all-roads-closed climax and requires every winning script to be revalidated.

claim: In the three-player game seat 2 receives only five activations for the same three-book load as seat 1 receives six, and sets B, J, and P give that seat two long legs whose shortest completion consumes all four pre-delivery movement opportunities, so one forced short crossing breaks that mode while the two- and four-player schedules retain more slack; this is medium because the mode is solvable but markedly less tolerant of the closure system it is meant to showcase.
where: Players and time; Edge cases; dispatch_card.set_manifest.3_player
fix_tried: Use an 18-turn night at three players so every seat receives six activations, then retune those manifests for the extra round; this costs a player-count exception, a longer and easier three-player game, and one more rule to teach.

claim: Because every courier starts on its first book, every later destination is known from the full queue printed on its owner's card, and every successive leg is only two to four roads, most movement reduces to privately computing the shortest one- or two-step advance while every mandatory clue is mechanically determined; this is medium because the rotating peg choice survives but most seats repeatedly report rather than decide.
where: Setup steps 5-6; Turn structure phases 2-3; dispatch_card; satchel
fix_tried: Replace the current distance choice with an explicit tradeoff: a Careful move crosses one road and may shift one standing peg into either adjacent empty rim hole, while a Fast move crosses two roads and cannot shift a peg; this costs teach time, weakens closure pressure, and creates an unmeasured balance tail between the two options.

claim: At three players the fixed sixteenth activation always belongs to seat 1, giving that seat the only chance to make or repair a final delivery after every other seat is out of turns; this is low because the game is cooperative and some manifests finish earlier, but the last meaningful activation is still assigned by seat order.
fix_tried: Adopt the same 18-turn three-player clock so all seats receive six activations, or if the 16-turn clock is retained rotate which seat receives the extra activation and compensate the skipped seat on the next game; either fix costs a count-specific timing rule, and rotation costs one more rule to teach without removing within-game asymmetry.
